claim: Maintaining paternal Western diet feeding for five consecutive generations in mice induces an enhancement in fat mass over generations.
source: Here, we show that maintaining paternal Western diet feeding for five consecutive generations in mice induces an enhancement in fat mass and related metabolic diseases over generations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Maintaining paternal Western diet feeding for five consecutive generations in mice induces related metabolic diseases over generations.
source: Here, we show that maintaining paternal Western diet feeding for five consecutive generations in mice induces an enhancement in fat mass and related metabolic diseases over generations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Chow-diet-fed progenies from multigenerational Western-diet-fed males develop a 'healthy' overweight phenotype characterized by normal glucose metabolism.
source: Strikingly, chow-diet-fed progenies from these multigenerational Western-diet-fed males develop a 'healthy' overweight phenotype characterized by normal glucose metabolism and without fatty liver that persists for four subsequent generations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Chow-diet-fed progenies from multigenerational Western-diet-fed males develop a 'healthy' overweight phenotype without fatty liver.
source: Strikingly, chow-diet-fed progenies from these multigenerational Western-diet-fed males develop a 'healthy' overweight phenotype characterized by normal glucose metabolism and without fatty liver that persists for four subsequent generations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The 'healthy' overweight phenotype in chow-diet-fed progenies from multigenerational Western-diet-fed males persists for four subsequent generations.
source: Strikingly, chow-diet-fed progenies from these multigenerational Western-diet-fed males develop a 'healthy' overweight phenotype characterized by normal glucose metabolism and without fatty liver that persists for four subsequent generations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Sperm RNAs are sufficient for establishment but not for long-term maintenance of epigenetic inheritance of metabolic pathologies.
source: Mechanistically, sperm RNA microinjection experiments into zygotes suggest that sperm RNAs are sufficient for establishment but not for long-term maintenance of epigenetic inheritance of metabolic pathologies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding based on microinjection experiments.

claim: Progressive and permanent metabolic deregulation induced by successive paternal Western-diet-fed generations may contribute to the worldwide epidemic of metabolic diseases.
source: Progressive and permanent metabolic deregulation induced by successive paternal Western-diet-fed generations may contribute to the worldwide epidemic of metabolic diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a speculative conclusion.

claim: Nongenetic inheritance of newly acquired phenotypes is a relatively new concept in biology.
source: Nongenetic inheritance of newly acquired phenotypes is a relatively new concept in biology whereby changes induced by specific environmental cues in parents (mothers and/or fathers) can be transmitted to the next generations (Chen et al., 2016; Fullston et al., 2013; Grandjean et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Changes induced by specific environmental cues in parents can be transmitted to the next generations.
source: Nongenetic inheritance of newly acquired phenotypes is a relatively new concept in biology whereby changes induced by specific environmental cues in parents (mothers and/or fathers) can be transmitted to the next generations (Chen et al., 2016; Fullston et al., 2013; Grandjean et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Nongenetic inheritance is evolutionarily conserved and has been described from worms to humans.
source: This process is evolutionarily conserved and has been described from worms to humans (Gapp et al., 2014; Portha et al., 2019; Remy, 2010; Skinner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Environmental cues have the potential to modify the molecular hereditary information carried by the spermatozoa.
source: The fact that environmental cues have the potential to modify the molecular hereditary information carried by the spermatozoa demonstrates that the environmentally induced epigenetic modifications (Agarwal and Majzoub, 2017) are not erased through the epigenetic reprogramming process, causing them to be inherited by the next generations (Carone et al., 2010; Soubry, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Environmentally induced epigenetic modifications are not erased through the epigenetic reprogramming process.
source: The fact that environmental cues have the potential to modify the molecular hereditary information carried by the spermatozoa demonstrates that the environmentally induced epigenetic modifications (Agarwal and Majzoub, 2017) are not erased through the epigenetic reprogramming process, causing them to be inherited by the next generations (Carone et al., 2010; Soubry, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Sperm RNA acts as a vector of paternal intergenerational epigenetic inheritance of environmentally induced metabolic pathologies.
source: Although the role of epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation (Carone et al., 2010; de Castro Barbosa et al., 2016; Ge et al., 2014) and chromatin modifications (Öst et al., 2014; Terashima et al., 2015) cannot be excluded in this process, independent experimental data strongly evoke the central role of sperm RNA as a vector of paternal intergenerational epigenetic inheritance of, at least, environmentally induced metabolic pathologies (Chen et al., 2016; Grandjean et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Environmentally induced epigenetic alterations are reversible, enabling the loss of previously acquired characteristics.
source: Unlike genetic inheritance, environmentally induced epigenetic alterations are reversible, enabling the loss of previously acquired characteristics (Cropley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Most reports on paternal environmental effects have been based on the maintenance of paternal environmental cues for just one generation.
source: Although environmental changes might persist over several generations, most reports have been based on the maintenance of paternal environmental cues for just one generation (Huypens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Multigenerational WD feeding exacerbates the increased body weight mass induced by this diet.
source: According to a previous study (Massiera et al., 2010), multigenerational WD feeding exacerbates the increased body weight mass induced by this diet.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: WD4 and WD5 males weighted significantly more than the WD1 and WD3 ones (p<0.05 and <0.01, respectively).
source: Despite marked heterogeneity in the WD4 and WD5 populations, we found that the WD4 and WD5 males weighted significantly more than the WD1 and WD3 ones (p<0.05 and <0.01, respectively) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Growing heterogeneity of the body weight mass between the males of the first and the latter generations was observed in the four independent families.
source: Interestingly, growing heterogeneity of the body weight mass between the males of the first and the latter generations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) was observed in the four independent families, indicating that the phenotypic heterogeneity previously observed in diet-induced obesity mouse models (Burcelin et al., 2002) increases progressively over the generations.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to a supplementary figure and a citation.

claim: Phenotypic heterogeneity in diet-induced obesity mouse models increases progressively over the generations.
source: Interestingly, growing heterogeneity of the body weight mass between the males of the first and the latter generations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) was observed in the four independent families, indicating that the phenotypic heterogeneity previously observed in diet-induced obesity mouse models (Burcelin et al., 2002) increases progressively over the generations.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The increase in total body weight with paternal multigenerational WD feeding was associated with an increase in perigonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) mass.
source: This increase in total body weight with paternal multigenerational WD feeding was associated with an increase in perigonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) mass (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: WD5 gWAT weighted significantly more than the WD1 gWAT (p<0.05).
source: Indeed, WD5 gWAT weighted significantly more than the WD1 gWAT (p<0.05) and the gWAT volume measured by computed tomography increased 2.3-fold and 3.4-fold in WD1 and WD5 mice, respectively, compared to that of control mice (CD-fed mice) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data.

claim: The gWAT volume measured by computed tomography increased 2.3-fold in WD1 mice compared to control mice.
source: Indeed, WD5 gWAT weighted significantly more than the WD1 gWAT (p<0.05) and the gWAT volume measured by computed tomography increased 2.3-fold and 3.4-fold in WD1 and WD5 mice, respectively, compared to that of control mice (CD-fed mice) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data.

claim: The gWAT volume measured by computed tomography increased 3.4-fold in WD5 mice compared to control mice.
source: Indeed, WD5 gWAT weighted significantly more than the WD1 gWAT (p<0.05) and the gWAT volume measured by computed tomography increased 2.3-fold and 3.4-fold in WD1 and WD5 mice, respectively, compared to that of control mice (CD-fed mice) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data.

claim: The increase in gWAT mass was positively correlated with total body weight (perigonadal fat mass versus total body weight; Spearman's r = 0.78, p<0.0001).
source: The increase in gWAT mass was positively correlated with total body weight (perigonadal fat mass versus total body weight; Spearman's r = 0.78, p<0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical values and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The increase in gWAT mass was associated with the hypertrophy of white adipocytes.
source: It was also associated with the hypertrophy of white adipocytes, with a median surface cell area of white adipocytes increasing from 1500 to 4000 μm2 from the first (WD1) to the fifth generation (WD5) and with a decreased calculated number of adipocytes in WD5 compared to the controls (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 1D-F.

claim: The median surface cell area of white adipocytes increased from 1500 to 4000 μm2 from WD1 to WD5.
source: It was also associated with the hypertrophy of white adipocytes, with a median surface cell area of white adipocytes increasing from 1500 to 4000 μm2 from the first (WD1) to the fifth generation (WD5) and with a decreased calculated number of adipocytes in WD5 compared to the controls (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 1D-F.

claim: There was a decreased calculated number of adipocytes in WD5 compared to the controls.
source: It was also associated with the hypertrophy of white adipocytes, with a median surface cell area of white adipocytes increasing from 1500 to 4000 μm2 from the first (WD1) to the fifth generation (WD5) and with a decreased calculated number of adipocytes in WD5 compared to the controls (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 1D-F.

claim: Multigenerational WD feeding has a strong impact on the gWAT gene expression profile.
source: Furthermore, our RNA-seq comparison between the gWAT of WD1 and WD5 males revealed that multigenerational WD feeding has a strong impact on the gWAT gene expression profile.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on RNA-seq data.

claim: There was an increase in differentially expressed genes (DEGs) from 325 in WD1 to 1199 in WD5 compared to the respective CD-fed mice.
source: In fact, we observed an increase in differentially expressed genes (DEGs), from 325 in WD1 (with 93 upregulated and 232 downregulated genes) to 1199 (757 upregulated and 442 downregulated) in WD5, compared to the respective CD-fed mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on RNA-seq data.

claim: The majority of DEGs in WD1 (66%) were also deregulated in WD5.
source: Interestingly, while the majority of DEGs in WD1 (66%) were also deregulated in WD5, a minority of DEGs in WD5 (only 8% for the upregulated genes and 35% for the downregulated genes) were deregulated in WD1 (p-value<0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on RNA-seq data.

claim: A minority of DEGs in WD5 (only 8% for the upregulated genes and 35% for the downregulated genes) were deregulated in WD1.
source: Interestingly, while the majority of DEGs in WD1 (66%) were also deregulated in WD5, a minority of DEGs in WD5 (only 8% for the upregulated genes and 35% for the downregulated genes) were deregulated in WD1 (p-value<0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on RNA-seq data.

claim: All common genes between WD1 and WD5 DEGs were deregulated in the same direction.
source: Importantly, all common genes were deregulated in the same direction (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1G.

claim: WD5 DEGs showed specific enrichment in gene sets associated with CHEN_METABOLIC_SYNDROM_NETWORK.
source: Interestingly, querying the WD1 and WD5 DEGs against the molecular signature database collection of curated gene pathway annotations revealed a specific WD5 enrichment in gene sets associated with CHEN_METABOLIC_SYNDROM_NETWORK (genes forming the macrophage-enriched metabolic network claimed to have a causal relationship with metabolic syndrome traits) and with genes potentially regulated by the methylation of lysine 4 (H3K4) and lysine 27 (H3K27) of histone H3 and by polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) (Figure 1—source data 2; Liberzon, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data and a citation.

claim: WD5 DEGs showed enrichment in genes potentially regulated by the methylation of lysine 4 (H3K4) and lysine 27 (H3K27) of histone H3 and by polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2).
source: Interestingly, querying the WD1 and WD5 DEGs against the molecular signature database collection of curated gene pathway annotations revealed a specific WD5 enrichment in gene sets associated with CHEN_METABOLIC_SYNDROM_NETWORK (genes forming the macrophage-enriched metabolic network claimed to have a causal relationship with metabolic syndrome traits) and with genes potentially regulated by the methylation of lysine 4 (H3K4) and lysine 27 (H3K27) of histone H3 and by polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) (Figure 1—source data 2; Liberzon, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data and a citation.

claim: C57BL6/J-strain male mice fed a WD diet for one generation failed to develop strong alterations in liver phenotype.
source: Strikingly, although the C57BL6/J-strain male mice fed a WD diet for one generation failed to develop strong alterations in liver phenotype (Schierwagen et al., 2015; AMDCC et al., 2005), major abnormalities were observed in WD5 liver, that is, organ weight, histological and biochemical parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Major abnormalities were observed in WD5 liver in organ weight, histological and biochemical parameters.
source: Strikingly, although the C57BL6/J-strain male mice fed a WD diet for one generation failed to develop strong alterations in liver phenotype (Schierwagen et al., 2015; AMDCC et al., 2005), major abnormalities were observed in WD5 liver, that is, organ weight, histological and biochemical parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The mass of the WD5 liver was significantly higher than that of the CD specimens.
source: Indeed, the mass of the WD5 liver (not that of the WD1 liver) was significantly higher than that of the CD specimens (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Histological and biochemical examinations revealed the presence of macrovesicular steatosis in WD5 liver.
source: Furthermore, unlike WD1 liver, histological and biochemical examinations revealed the presence of macrovesicular steatosis with significantly increased triglyceride (TG) levels in WD5 liver compared with CD liver (p<0.01, respectively) (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 2D-F.

claim: WD5 liver had significantly increased triglyceride (TG) levels compared with CD liver (p<0.01).
source: Furthermore, unlike WD1 liver, histological and biochemical examinations revealed the presence of macrovesicular steatosis with significantly increased triglyceride (TG) levels in WD5 liver compared with CD liver (p<0.01, respectively) (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 2D-F.

claim: The phenotype of WD5 livers exhibits typical features of fatty liver.
source: Therefore, the phenotype of WD5 livers exhibits typical features of fatty liver.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the liver data.

claim: Circulating plasma levels of leptin were significantly higher in the WD3, WD4, and WD5 groups compared to CD-fed mice.
source: In comparison with CD-fed mice, circulating plasma levels of leptin, C-reactive protein (CRP), one marker of inflammation, and total cholesterol were significantly higher in the WD3 (p<0.01), WD4 (p<0.05), and WD5 (p<0.01) groups but not in the WD1 (p=0.07) or WD2 (p=0.4) groups (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: Circulating plasma levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) were significantly higher in the WD3, WD4, and WD5 groups compared to CD-fed mice.
source: In comparison with CD-fed mice, circulating plasma levels of leptin, C-reactive protein (CRP), one marker of inflammation, and total cholesterol were significantly higher in the WD3 (p<0.01), WD4 (p<0.05), and WD5 (p<0.01) groups but not in the WD1 (p=0.07) or WD2 (p=0.4) groups (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: Circulating plasma levels of total cholesterol were significantly higher in the WD3, WD4, and WD5 groups compared to CD-fed mice.
source: In comparison with CD-fed mice, circulating plasma levels of leptin, C-reactive protein (CRP), one marker of inflammation, and total cholesterol were significantly higher in the WD3 (p<0.01), WD4 (p<0.05), and WD5 (p<0.01) groups but not in the WD1 (p=0.07) or WD2 (p=0.4) groups (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: The alterations in metabolic parameters in WD-fed males were found to be positively correlated with the increase in gWAT mass.
source: The alterations in these metabolic parameters in WD-fed males were found to be positively correlated with the increase in gWAT mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The increase in serum leptin in WD-fed males was positively correlated with an increase in leptin mRNA levels in the gWAT (total serum leptin and leptin mRNA, Spearman's r = 0.89, p<0.0001).
source: At the molecular level, the increase in serum leptin in WD-fed males was positively correlated with an increase in leptin mRNA levels in the gWAT of the respective male mice (total serum leptin and leptin mRNA, Spearman's r = 0.89, p<0.0001, Figure 1—figure supplement 2I), suggesting an accumulation of epigenetic modifications at the leptin promoter.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical values and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Leptin upregulation occurs via epigenetic malprogramming in white adipose tissue.
source: These results are in line with recent studies showing that leptin upregulation occurs via epigenetic malprogramming in white adipose tissue (Lecoutre et al., 2017; Masuyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: A significantly impaired response in the intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test (GTT) was found in all WD-fed mouse groups.
source: Furthermore, we found a significantly impaired response in the intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test (GTT) in all WD-fed mouse groups (Figure 2A), which was not associated, except for in WD2-fed males, with an impaired insulin response, as shown by the intraperitoneal insulin tolerance test (ITT) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The impaired glucose tolerance in WD-fed mice was not associated with an impaired insulin response, except for in WD2-fed males.
source: Furthermore, we found a significantly impaired response in the intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test (GTT) in all WD-fed mouse groups (Figure 2A), which was not associated, except for in WD2-fed males, with an impaired insulin response, as shown by the intraperitoneal insulin tolerance test (ITT) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: There was no significant exacerbation of insulin sensitivity in successive generations.
source: Therefore, unlike the other metabolic parameters, we did not notice any significant exacerbation of insulin sensitivity in successive generations.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The response to an intraperitoneal GTT was not correlated with the gWAT mass.
source: Moreover, the response to an intraperitoneal GTT (measured through the area under the curve [AUC]-GTT calculation) was not correlated with the gWAT mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a supplementary figure.

claim: Male and female F1 progenies derived from WD1 males (F1-WD1) were statistically heavier than the control animals with CD-fed ancestors.
source: As expected from previous studies (Fullston et al., 2013; Grandjean et al., 2016), male and female F1 progenies derived from WD1 males (F1-WD1) were statistically heavier than the control animals with CD-fed ancestors (Figure 3B, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and figures.

claim: The overweight phenotype in F1-WD1 progenies was associated with impaired glucose tolerance as measured by the GTT for both male and female F1-WD1 progenies.
source: This overweight phenotype was associated with impaired glucose tolerance as measured by the GTT for both the male F1-WD1 and F1-WD5 progenies and the female F1-WD5 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, G, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: There was an absence of intergenerational inheritance of the fatty liver phenotype observed in the WD1 and WD5 progenitors.
source: We noticed, however, the absence of intergenerational inheritance of the fatty liver phenotype observed in the WD1 and WD5 progenitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a supplementary figure.

claim: Both male F2-WD1 and F2-WD5 CD-fed progenies were overweight (p<0.01).
source: Both male F2-WD1 and F2-WD5 CD-fed progenies were also overweight (p<0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The overweight phenotype in F2 progenies was associated with an excessive accruement of gWAT mass of at least 90% over the control.
source: This phenotype was associated with an excessive accruement of gWAT mass of at least 90% over the control (Figure 3C, E, G, I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figures.

claim: The female and male F2-WD5 progenies were significantly fatter and heavier than the F2-WD1 cohorts.
source: Importantly, although the female and male F2-WD5 progenies were found to be significantly fatter and heavier than the F2-WD1 cohorts, these mice did not exhibit impaired glucose tolerance (as measured by the GTT) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, G) or signs of fatty liver lesions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: F2-WD5 progenies did not exhibit impaired glucose tolerance or signs of fatty liver lesions.
source: Importantly, although the female and male F2-WD5 progenies were found to be significantly fatter and heavier than the F2-WD1 cohorts, these mice did not exhibit impaired glucose tolerance (as measured by the GTT) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, G) or signs of fatty liver lesions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The populations of males and females of the F3-WD1 progenies were very homogeneous, exhibiting metabolic characteristics very similar to control mice.
source: Thus, as illustrated in Figure 3B–I, the populations of males and females of the F3-WD1 progenies were very homogeneous, exhibiting metabolic characteristics very similar to control mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figures.

claim: Both populations of males and females of the F3-WD5 progenies were heterogeneous in terms of body and gWAT weights.
source: By contrast, both populations of males and females of the F3-WD5 progenies were heterogeneous in terms of body and gWAT weights, some of them showing weights closed to CD mice and others being clearly overweight and fat.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Both F3-WD5 populations were significantly heavier and fatter (p<0.001 and <0.01, respectively) than control and F3-WD1 populations.
source: However, both F3-WD5 populations were significantly heavier and fatter (p<0.001 and <0.01, respectively) than control and F3-WD1 populations (Figure 3B–I, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figures.

claim: The progenies derived from WD5-fed animals did not display any alterations in terms of glucose metabolism at 4 months of age.
source: Strikingly, despite being overweight, the progenies derived from WD5-fed animals did not display any alterations in terms of glucose metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H) and fatty liver pathologies at 4 months of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The progenies derived from WD5-fed animals did not display fatty liver pathologies at 4 months of age.
source: Strikingly, despite being overweight, the progenies derived from WD5-fed animals did not display any alterations in terms of glucose metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H) and fatty liver pathologies at 4 months of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: WD feeding for multiple generations induces stable germline epigenetic modifications that were not erased after removing the stressor(s) for at least four generations of CD-fed progeny.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that WD feeding for multiple generations induces stable germline epigenetic modifications that were not erased after removing the stressor(s) for at least four generations of CD-fed progeny.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the progeny data.

claim: Specific signatures of sperm small non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs) from WD-fed mice act as a vector of intergenerational epigenetic inheritance of newly acquired pathologies.
source: Specific signatures of sperm small non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs) from WD-fed mice have been previously shown to act as a vector of intergenerational epigenetic inheritance of newly acquired pathologies (Chen et al., 2016; Grandjean et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016; Sarker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: A sperm RNA signature specifically induced in the first generation of WD-diet males is characterized by an increase in the proportion of rsRNA.
source: We found a sperm RNA signature that is specifically induced in the first generation of WD-diet males characterized by an increase in the proportion of rsRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on sequencing data.

claim: The sncRNA signature observed in the first generation of WD-fed male tends to disappear in the fifth generation of WD-fed male.
source: Strikingly, this sncRNA signature observed in the first generation of WD-fed male fed a WD tends to disappear in the fifth generation of WD-fed male, which exhibit a sncRNAs signature very similar to that of CD sncRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on sequencing data.

claim: ~64% of the sncRNAs were annotated to rsRNAs in WD1, while only ~40% of them were annotated to rsRNAs in CD and WD5 sperm.
source: On the one hand, while ~64% of the sncRNAs were annotated to rsRNAs in WD1, only ~40% of them were annotated to rsRNAs in CD and WD5 sperm (Figure 4D), suggesting a global modification of the sncRNA population upon WD exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: 479 DEGs were identified in WD1 sperm compared to control mice.
source: Indeed, searching for small RNA DEGs (adjusted p value<0.05) between WD (WD1 or WD5) and CD sperm, we identified 479 and 66 DEGs in WD1 and WD5, respectively, compared to control mice (Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: 66 DEGs were identified in WD5 sperm compared to control mice.
source: Indeed, searching for small RNA DEGs (adjusted p value<0.05) between WD (WD1 or WD5) and CD sperm, we identified 479 and 66 DEGs in WD1 and WD5, respectively, compared to control mice (Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: The majority of WD5 DEGs (47 out of 66) were already deregulated in WD1.
source: Interestingly, the majority of WD5 DEGs (47 out of 66) were already deregulated in WD1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Among the common sncRNAs between WD1 and WD5, tsRNA and microRNAs known to be involved in short-term epigenetic inheritance of metabolic dysfunction were identified.
source: Among these common sncRNAs, we identified tsRNA and microRNAs known to be involved in short-term epigenetic inheritance of metabolic dysfunction (intergenerational inheritance) (Chen et al., 2016; Grandjean et al., 2016; Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and figures.

claim: No sncRNA was found deregulated (adjusted p<0.05) between WD1 and WD5.
source: Interestingly, no sncRNA was found deregulated (adjusted p<0.05) between WD1 and WD5.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The sensitivity of sperm sncRNA signature to diet is modulated by the diet of ancestors.
source: These data indicate that the sensitivity of sperm sncRNA signature to diet, observed independently by several groups (Nätt et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018), is also modulated by the diet of ancestors.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Male 12-week F1-RNA-WD1 and F1-RNA-WD5 progenies were heavier than F1-RNA-CD progenies (31 g vs. 30 g, p<0.05).
source: In agreement with previous studies, male 12-week F1-RNA-WD1 and F1-RNA-WD5 progenies were heavier than F1-RNA-CD progenies (31 g vs. 30 g, p<0.05) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: F1-RNA-WD1 and F1-RNA-WD5 progenies displayed glucose and insulin response alterations, as shown by GTT and ITT analyses.
source: In addition, they displayed glucose and insulin response alterations, as shown by GTT and ITT analyses, with significantly higher values of the AUC to controls (Figure 5D, E, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by figures.

claim: Neither abnormal TG levels nor histological abnormalities were observed in liver from F1-RNA-CD and F1-RNA-WD progenies.
source: Regarding the fatty liver phenotype, neither abnormal TG levels nor histological abnormalities were observed in liver from F1-RNA-CD and F1-RNA-WD progenies.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Overweight phenotypes and glucose response alterations were partially transmitted to the F2 and F3 generations in RNA microinjection experiments.
source: Overweight phenotypes and glucose response alterations were partially transmitted to the F2 and F3 generations (Figure 5—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data.

claim: Total body weight mass of the F2-RNA-WD males was significantly heavier than that of the F2-RNA-CD male (p<0.05).
source: Indeed, total body weight mass of the F2-RNA-WD males was significantly heavier than that of the F2-RNA-CD male (p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The metabolic abnormality in RNA-WD progenies did not persist in the F3 and F4 progenies.
source: This metabolic abnormality did not persist in the F3 and F4 progenies.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Liver histological examinations revealed macro- and microvesicular steatosis in hepatocytes of two F2-WD overweight males (2 out of 10).
source: Intriguingly, while we did not observe any liver abnormalities in F1-RNA progenies, liver histological examinations revealed macro- and microvesicular steatosis in hepatocytes of two F2-WD overweight males (2 out of 10) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a supplementary figure.

claim: All the metabolic alterations in RNA-microinjected progenies were completely absent in the F4 generations.
source: Nevertheless, all the metabolic alterations were completely absent in the F4 generations (Figure 5—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data.

claim: The overweight phenotype induced by sperm RNA from WD5 males was not exacerbated compared to that induced by sperm RNA from WD1 males.
source: First, the overweight phenotype induced by sperm RNA from WD5 males was not exacerbated compared to that induced by sperm RNA from WD1 males.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a comparison of RNA microinjection results.

claim: No statistically significant difference was observed among the body weight of the F1, F2, and F3 progenies derived from sperm RNA of WD1- and WD5 animals.
source: In fact, no statistically significant difference was observed among the body weight of the F1, F2, and F3 progenies derived from sperm RNA of WD1- and WD5 animals.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The sperm-RNA-induced overweight phenotype was associated with glucose metabolic alterations (total body weight and AUC-GTT, Spearman's r = 0.4, p<0.01).
source: Second, the sperm-RNA-induced overweight phenotype was associated with glucose metabolic alterations (total body weight and AUC-GTT, Spearman's r = 0.4, p<0.01, Figure 5F) and was sporadically associated with fatty liver abnormalities in both WD1 and WD5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical values and reference to a figure.

claim: Sperm RNAs can unequivocally induce intergenerational phenotype but may induce some transgenerational features, although the effect is weaker than the effect induced by whole sperm.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that sperm RNAs can unequivocally induce intergenerational phenotype but may induce some transgenerational features, although the effect is weaker than the effect induced by whole sperm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the microinjection experiments.

claim: Sperm RNA injection can induce phenotype in both F1 and F2 generations in a psychological-stress-induced model.
source: This is in line with previous study using a psychological-stress-induced model showing that sperm RNA injection can also induce phenotype in both F1 and F2 generations (Gapp et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The sperm-RNA-induced overweight phenotype was not inherited for more than two generations.
source: Last, in contrast to natural mating of WD5, the sperm-RNA-induced overweight phenotype was not inherited for more than two generations.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Sperm RNAs are not sufficient for the long-term epigenetic inheritance of metabolic dysfunctions.
source: Together, these results indicate that sperm RNAs are not sufficient for the long-term epigenetic inheritance of metabolic dysfunctions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the microinjection experiments.

claim: Maintaining a WD for several generations promotes a progressive accumulation of epigenetic alterations in somatic and germ cells throughout generations.
source: In summary, our findings reveal that maintaining a WD for several generations promotes a progressive accumulation of epigenetic alterations in somatic and germ cells throughout generations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Ancestral exposure influences the magnitude of the overweight phenotype.
source: First, ancestral exposure influences the magnitude of the overweight phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: A male whose father, grandfather, great grandfather, great-great-grandfather, and great-great-great grandfather, up to five generations of exposure, have been fed a WD exhibits the most severe overweight phenotype associated with serious metabolic alterations.
source: Indeed, a male whose father, grandfather, great grandfather, great-great-grandfather, and great-great-great grandfather, up to five generations of exposure, have been fed a WD exhibits the most severe overweight phenotype associated with serious metabolic alterations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The father's ancestral history affected the pattern of inheritance of metabolic pathologies.
source: Second, the father's ancestral history (whether his ancestors were fed an unbalanced diet) affected the pattern of inheritance of this metabolic pathology.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Metabolic heterogeneity induced by an unbalanced diet has been reported in mice.
source: Metabolic heterogeneity induced by an unbalanced diet has already been reported in mice (Burcelin et al., 2002; Dumas et al., 2017), and the strong heterogeneity observed in our model may indicate an adaptative process whereby different subpopulations could emerge in response to the maintenance of an unbalanced diet.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The development of type 2 diabetes is positively associated with body weight.
source: Although it is well described that the development of type 2 diabetes is positively associated with body weight (Golay and Ybarra, 2005), we did not observe a strong correlation between fat mass and glucose and insulin sensitivities in males obtained after multigenerational WD feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Hepatic steatosis increased in severity with successive generations of a WD.
source: However, we identified one obese-associated pathology that increased in severity with successive generations of a WD, namely, hepatic steatosis, indicating that exposure sensitivity is heightened by multiple generations of exposure, at least for this diet-associated pathology.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The family food environment, parental dietary behaviors, and family obesity might be an additional clue to explain the increasing incidence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in humans.
source: Thus, the family food environment, parental dietary behaviors, and family obesity might be an additional clue to explain the increasing incidence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in humans (Kumar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Multiple generations of WD exposure impact the hereditary makeup.
source: Importantly, multiple generations of WD exposure impact not only the sensitivity to a WD but also the hereditary makeup, also called background.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: When the father has no WD-fed ancestor, the fatness of its progenies tends to disappear after WD removal.
source: Indeed, when the father has no WD-fed ancestor, the fatness of its progenies tends to disappear after WD removal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: In the case of fathers with several WD-fed ancestors, the progenies will remain stably overweight for more than four generations.
source: However, in the case of fathers with several WD-fed ancestors, the progenies will remain stably overweight for more than four generations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The male progenies of the third and fourth generations of WD5 males were overweight but did not develop metabolic alterations, such as glucose/insulin sensitivity alterations and fatty liver diseases.
source: Intriguingly, although the male progenies of the third and fourth generations of WD5 males were overweight, they did not develop metabolic alterations, such as glucose/insulin sensitivity alterations and fatty liver diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The combination of ancestral and individual diet exposure was both necessary and sufficient to elicit the most severe metabolic effects in mice.
source: Together, these data strongly suggest that the combination of ancestral and individual diet exposure was both necessary and sufficient to elicit the most severe metabolic effects in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The five-generational WD-fed males have evolved to develop a protective mechanism in glucose and liver fat metabolism that can be inherited by the offspring.
source: Thus, it looks like the five-generational WD-fed males have evolved to develop a protective mechanism in glucose and liver fat metabolism that can be inherited by the offspring.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative conclusion.

claim: In guppies, a wide range of plastic responses under different light conditions were observed, which were dependent on multigenerational exposure to different light environments.
source: For instance, in guppies, a wide range of plastic responses under different light conditions were observed, which were dependent on multigenerational exposure to different light environments (Kranz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: In mites, zinc element sensitivity increased by continuous multigenerational exposure.
source: In mites, zinc element sensitivity increased by continuous multigenerational exposure (Jegede et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: In mice, male sensitivity to environmental estrogens was enhanced by successive generations of exposure.
source: In mice, male sensitivity to environmental estrogens was enhanced by successive generations of exposure (Horan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Rats undernourished for 50 generations showed multiple metabolic alterations that were not reversed in their respective F1 and F2 CD-fed progenies.
source: Finally, rats undernourished for 50 generations showed multiple metabolic alterations that were not reversed in their respective F1 and F2 CD-fed progenies (Hardikar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The exacerbation of stress-induced phenotypes upon multigeneration exposure as well as the stabilization of newly induced phenotypes is an evolutionarily conserved process.
source: Together, the present and previously published studies indicate that the exacerbation of stress-induced phenotypes upon multigeneration exposure as well as the stabilization of newly induced phenotypes is an evolutionarily conserved process.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study and cited literature.

claim: sncRNAs signature is not only the reflect of the diet of the father, but also that of the diet of the ancestors.
source: Indeed, on the one hand, we showed that sncRNAs signature is not only the reflect of the diet of the father, as already demonstrated (Nätt et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018), but also that of the diet of the ancestors (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Small RNAs are vectors of intergenerational inheritance but are not sufficient for the long-term inheritance of diet-induced metabolic alterations.
source: On the other hand, our microinjection experiments showed that small RNAs are vectors of intergenerational inheritance but are not sufficient for the long-term inheritance of diet-induced metabolic alterations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the microinjection experiments.

claim: All mouse experiments were conducted in accordance with the National and European legislations for the care and use of research animals.
source: All mouse experiments were conducted in accordance with the National and European legislations for the care and use of research animals.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.
